title: Choose the visual world
question: The roll assigned Safety Card. Keep it, take an alternate, or re-roll. Hanken Grotesk and JetBrains Mono stay in every option.

options.label: Safety Card
options.thesis: Every option is a numbered panel: the safe one is ticked, the unsafe ones are crossed out.
options.viewport: Top bar with disruption picker and Run. A yellow answer panel leads: +20 min, gate B10, land 16:08, Approve. Slot panels below, with blocked ones crossed out; negotiation log on the right.
options.risk: Heavy crosses and yellow can feel loud over a long shift.

raised.raise: Slots and rules pack as whole keyed cells, never loose cards.
Only what can be pressed takes the action colour.
Every slot shows its minutes against the fuel limit, a budget that cannot overflow.
All slot panels hold one exact scale on a shared baseline, so they compare directly.

options.label: Airport Wayfinding
options.thesis: The decision is a terminal sign: gate, time and direction readable from across the room.
options.viewport: Black top bar with picker and Run. A full-width yellow sign states gate B10 and landing 16:08, with Approve beside it; slots and log sit in plain panels below.
options.risk: The most familiar answer for anything airport-related; it may read as an airport theme.

options.label: Midnight Transit Diagram
options.thesis: ATC, pilot and ground are three coloured lines that meet at one interchange: the agreed plan.
options.viewport: Dark shell with picker and Run. A line diagram across the top: slots are stations, blocked ones suspended, three lines converging on the plan. Plan and Approve at right.
options.case: Strongest at showing the negotiation; holds audience identification, since airline people read route maps daily, but the verdict reads more slowly than a panel.
options.risk: Delay minutes are not a route, so the metaphor needs care to stay honest.

options.label: Split-Flap Board
options.thesis: Each slot is a board row, and the plan flips into place as the checker passes it.
options.viewport: Dark shell with picker and Run. A sortable table of slots in flap-style cells: time, gate, status. The chosen row is lit, with Approve beside it; log on the right.
options.case: Holds audience identification and suits the flip motion, but it is nearly the dark look you are replacing and risks a costume.
options.risk: Close to a cliché, and closest to the current dark interface.

options.label: Convention Catalog
options.thesis: Options as stamp-sized keyed cells packed on one sheet.
options.viewport: A dense numbered grid of options.
options.case: Loses both axes: duty managers do not know this world, and the verdict gets buried.
options.kept: Density courage: whole keyed cells instead of loose cards.

options.label: Warm Consumer App
options.thesis: Soft cards, plain labels and one action colour.
options.viewport: Stacked soft cards with a bottom bar.
options.case: Loses both axes: too casual for a safety decision and no sense of operations.
options.kept: Action colour appears only on what can be pressed.
options.risk: Feels like a toy for a safety call.

options.label: Cassette J-Card
options.thesis: A hand-ruled listing timed to fit the tape.
options.case: Loses both axes: no link to the audience, and handwriting undermines trust.
options.kept: A hard budget: every item is timed against a limit that cannot overflow.

options.label: Botanical Folio
options.thesis: One subject compared across registered plates.
options.viewport: Slots as aligned plates on one baseline.
options.case: Loses both axes: foreign to operations and too slow to read.
options.kept: Registration: every plate keeps one scale and baseline for direct comparison.
options.risk: Decorative; reads as a museum piece.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A clean operations dashboard, the way this category ships it, executed well.
canonCard.viewport: Side navigation, a metrics row, plan card and log, all standard components.
canonCard.risk: Dependable but plain, and you said bland is what would feel wrong.
